segments.speaker: ADAM
segments.en: So, Michelle, shall we make a start on our presentation? We haven’t got that much time left.

segments.speaker: MICHELLE
segments.en: No, Adam. But at least we’ve done all the background reading. I found it really interesting – I’d never even heard of the Laki eruption before this.

segments.speaker: ADAM
segments.en: Me neither. I suppose 1783 is a long time ago.

segments.speaker: MICHELLE
segments.en: But it was a huge eruption and it had such devastating consequences.

segments.speaker: ADAM
segments.en: I know. It was great there were so many primary sources to look at. It really gives you a sense of how catastrophic the volcano was. People were really trying to make sense of the science for the first time.

segments.speaker: MICHELLE
segments.en: That’s right. But what I found more significant was how it impacted directly and indirectly on political events, as well as having massive social and economic consequences.

segments.speaker: ADAM
segments.en: I know. That should be the main focus of our presentation.

segments.speaker: MICHELLE
segments.en: The observations made by people at the time were interesting, weren’t they? I mean, they all gave a pretty consistent account of what happened, even if they didn’t always use the same terminology.

segments.speaker: ADAM
segments.en: Yeah. I was surprised there were so many weather stations established by that time – so, you know, you can see how the weather changed, often by the hour.

segments.speaker: MICHELLE
segments.en: Right. Writers at the time talked about the Laki haze to describe the volcanic fog that spread across Europe. They all realised that this wasn’t the sort of fog they were used to – and of course this was in pre-industrial times- so they hadn’t experienced sulphur-smelling fog before.

segments.speaker: ADAM
segments.en: No, that’s true.

segments.speaker: MICHELLE
segments.en: Reports from the period blamed the haze for an increase in headaches, respiratory issues and asthma attacks. And they all describe how it covered the sun and made it look a strange red colour.

segments.speaker: ADAM
segments.en: Must have been very weird.

segments.speaker: MICHELLE
segments.en: It’s interesting that Benjamin Franklin wrote about the haze. Did you read that? He was the American ambassador in Paris at the time.

segments.speaker: ADAM
segments.en: Yeah. At first no one realised that the haze was caused by the volcanic eruption in Iceland.

segments.speaker: MICHELLE
segments.en: It was Benjamin Franklin who realised that before anyone else.

segments.speaker: ADAM
segments.en: He’s often credited with that, apparently. But a French naturalist beat him to it – I can’t remember his name. I’d have to look it up. Then other naturalists had the same idea – all independently of each other.

segments.speaker: MICHELLE
segments.en: Oh right. We should talk about the immediate impact of the eruption, which was obviously enormous- especially in Iceland, where so many people died.

segments.speaker: ADAM
segments.en: Mmm. You’d expect that- and the fact that the volcanic ash drifted so swiftly – but not that the effects would go on for so long. Or that two years after the eruption, strange weather events were being reported as far away as North America and North Africa. /26

segments.speaker: MICHELLE
segments.en: No. I found all that hard to believe too. It must have been terrible- and there was nothing anyone could do about it, even if they knew the ash cloud was coming in their direction. ——

segments.speaker: MICHELLE
segments.en: We should run through some of the terrible consequences of the eruption experienced in different countries. There’s quite a varied range.

segments.speaker: ADAM
segments.en: Starting with Iceland, where the impact on farming was devastating.

segments.speaker: MICHELLE
segments.en: Mmm. One of the most dramatic things there was the effect on livestock as they grazed in the fields. They were poisoned because they ate vegetation that had been contaminated with fluorine as a result of the volcanic fallout.

segments.speaker: ADAM
segments.en: That was horrible. In Egypt, the bizarre weather patterns led to a severe drought and as a result the Nile didn’t flood, which meant the crops all failed.

segments.speaker: MICHELLE
segments.en: It’s so far from where the eruption happened and yet the famine there led to more people dying than any other country. It was worse than the plague.

segments.speaker: ADAM
segments.en: OK. Then in the UK the mortality rate went up a lot- presumably from respiratory illnesses. According to one report it was about double the usual number and included an unusually high percentage of people under the age of 25.

segments.speaker: MICHELLE
segments.en: Mmm. I think people will be surprised to hear that the weather in the USA was badly affected too. George Washington even makes a note in his diary that they were snowbound until March in Virginia. That was before he became president.

segments.speaker: ADAM
segments.en: Yes, and there was ice floating down the Mississippi, which was unprecedented.

segments.speaker: MICHELLE
segments.en: Astonishing, really. Anyway, what do you think ...

SECTION 3
Questions 21-30
LAKI ERUPTION OF 1783
Choose the correct letter A, B or C.
Questions:
    Q Num: 21
    Text: Why do the students think the Laki eruption of 1783 is so important?
    Options:
        It was the most severe eruption in modern times.
        It led to the formal study of volcanoes.
        It had a profound effect on society.
    Q Num: 22
    Text: What surprised Adam about observations made at the time?
    Options:
        the number of places producing them.
        the contradictions in them.
        the lack of scientific data to support them.
    Q Num: 23
    Text: According to Michelle, what did the contemporary sources say about the Laki 'haze'?
    Options:
        People thought it was similar to ordinary fog.
        It was associated with health issues.
        It completely blocked out the sun for weeks.
    Q Num: 24
    Text: Adam corrects Michelle when she claims that Benjamin Franklin
    Options:
        came to the wrong conclusion about the cause of the haze.
        was the first to identify the reason for the haze.
        supported the opinions of other observers about the haze.
Choose TWO letters A–E.
Q Num: 25
Text: Which TWO issues following the Laki eruption surprised the students?
Count: 2
Options:
    Id: A
    Text: how widespread the effects were
    Id: B
    Text: how long-lasting the effects were
    Id: C
    Text: the number of deaths it caused
    Id: D
    Text: the speed at which the volcanic ash cloud spread
    Id: E
    Text: how people ignored the warning signs
